passage.title: Blue Ribbon Peaches
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
I held the warm ceramic baking dish with both oven mitts as Mom opened the screen door of the county fair pavilion. Inside the bright hall, long tables gleamed with white paper cloths and rows of fancy desserts. Right away, my stomach did a nervous flip. The other bakers had brought towering three-layer cakes topped with spun sugar curls and glossy fruit tarts that looked like museum art. My entry was Aunt Delia's skillet peach cobbler, baked in a scratched blue dish that had seen twenty summers.

As I walked to Table Four, I wished I had piped whipped cream roses around the edge to hide the rustic crust. Unlike those tall bakery cakes with their smooth frosting, my cobbler had a bumpy golden top where sweet peach juice bubbled through the cracks. I set my dish beside a tall chocolate pie and quickly stepped back behind the rope. Soon the three judges walked over with their clipboards. I stared down at my shoes and waited for them to pass right by my plain square pan.

First, the head judge in the red apron tasted the tall cakes at the end of the row. She took polite little bites and wrote short notes on her pad without smiling. Then the judges stopped in front of my scratched blue dish. The golden peach cobbler, seasoned with a pinch of grated nutmeg and fresh lemon peel, was eagerly sampled by the head judge with a silver spoon. As soon as she tasted the warm fruit and crisp crust, her eyebrows rose in surprise.

Instead of moving on, she tapped her spoon against the dish and asked the other two judges to try a bite right away. I watched in shock as all three judges smiled and nodded together. The head judge looked across the rope, spotted the flour smudge on my sleeve, and gave me a warm wink. She said that fancy frosting looks pretty under bright lights, but nothing beats fresh Georgia peaches baked until the crust sings.

Ten minutes later, a shiny blue ribbon for First Place Youth Baking hung beside Aunt Delia's old dish. Walking out into the sunny fairgrounds, I felt silly for doubting our family recipe just because it lacked tall sugar curls. My plain cobbler did not need to copy a store window to be special. Sharing the honest flavor of home had been my strongest asset all along.

tier2Words.definition: a large open building or hall used for fairs, shows, and community events
tier2Words.rootHint: From Latin papilio, meaning 'large tent or butterfly wing'
tier2Words.contextClue: Mom opened the screen door of the county fair hall where long tables held rows of desserts.

tier2Words.definition: simple, homemade, and natural in style rather than fancy or polished
tier2Words.rootHint: From Latin rus, meaning 'countryside or farm'
tier2Words.contextClue: Unlike the smooth bakery cakes, the cobbler had a simple, bumpy golden top in an old family dish.

tier2Words.definition: tasted or tried a small portion of food to judge its quality
tier2Words.rootHint: From Old French essample, meaning 'small test piece'
tier2Words.contextClue: The head judge used a silver spoon to taste a bite of the warm fruit and crisp crust.

tier2Words.definition: a valuable strength or useful quality that helps someone succeed
tier2Words.rootHint: From Old French asez, meaning 'enough or valuable resource'
tier2Words.contextClue: Sharing the honest flavor of home turned out to be the narrator's greatest strength in the contest.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 3:

"The golden peach cobbler, seasoned with a pinch of grated nutmeg and fresh lemon peel, was eagerly sampled by the head judge with a silver spoon."

Based on the structure of the sentence, who or what sampled the golden peach cobbler?

options.text: The head judge sampled the golden peach cobbler with a silver spoon.
The golden peach cobbler sampled the silver spoon on Table Four.
A pinch of grated nutmeg sampled the fresh lemon peel.
Aunt Delia sampled the three-layer cake behind the rope.

questions.provingSentenceText: The golden peach cobbler, seasoned with a pinch of grated nutmeg and fresh lemon peel, was eagerly sampled by the head judge with a silver spoon.
questions.childTip: Look for the 'by' phrase right after 'was eagerly sampled' to see who tasted the cobbler.
questions.parentExplanation: In this passive-voice sentence, 'The golden peach cobbler' receives the action, while 'by the head judge' identifies the actor who sampled it.

questions.provingSentenceText: Unlike those tall bakery cakes with their smooth frosting, my cobbler had a bumpy golden top where sweet peach juice bubbled through the cracks.
questions.childTip: Notice the contrast word 'Unlike' in the next sentence: the crust is bumpy and simple compared to smooth bakery cakes.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 2 contrasts the 'rustic crust' with 'those tall bakery cakes with their smooth frosting,' showing that 'rustic' means simple, natural, and homemade.

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 1, why does the narrator feel nervous as soon as she walks into the county fair pavilion?

options.text: She realizes she forgot to add nutmeg and lemon peel to her peach cobbler.
She drops the warm ceramic dish on the floor before reaching Table Four.
She sees fancy cakes and tarts that make her family's cobbler look plain by comparison.
She learns that youth bakers are only allowed to enter chocolate pies in the contest.

questions.provingSentenceText: The other bakers had brought towering three-layer cakes topped with spun sugar curls and glossy fruit tarts that looked like museum art.
questions.childTip: Click the sentence in Paragraph 1 that describes what the other bakers had brought to the tables.
questions.parentExplanation: In Paragraph 1, the narrator's stomach does a nervous flip because the other entries are fancy three-layer cakes and glossy tarts that look like museum art compared to her cobbler in a scratched dish.

questions.prompt: How does the narrator's first-person point of view influence how the events at the baking contest are described?

options.text: It proves that the narrator does not care at all about winning a ribbon at the county fair.
It reveals the exact scores that each of the three judges writes down on their private clipboards.
It explains the step-by-step history of how the county fair pavilion was built twenty summers ago.
It lets the reader experience the narrator's secret doubts about her plain dish before she discovers how much the judges love its taste.

questions.provingSentenceText: As I walked to Table Four, I wished I had piped whipped cream roses around the edge to hide the rustic crust.
questions.childTip: Think about what 'I' lets us know: we hear the baker's worried thoughts inside her head before the judges taste her dish.
questions.parentExplanation: Because the story is told from the baker's first-person ('I') perspective (ELAGSE5RL6), readers directly share her initial insecurity about her cobbler's appearance and her surprise when its flavor wins first place.

questions.prompt: Part A: Which statement best expresses the central theme of the story?

options.text: True quality and honest family traditions matter more than flashy outward appearances.
Three-layer cakes with spun sugar curls never taste good at a summer fair.
Bakers must always buy brand-new ceramic dishes if they want to impress county fair judges.
Whipped cream roses are the easiest way to fix a dessert that has a bumpy crust.

questions.provingSentenceText: She said that fancy frosting looks pretty under bright lights, but nothing beats fresh Georgia peaches baked until the crust sings.
questions.childTip: Look at what the head judge says in Paragraph 4 and what the narrator realizes in Paragraph 5.
questions.parentExplanation: Both the head judge's remark in Paragraph 4 and the narrator's reflection in Paragraph 5 highlight the theme that genuine quality ('honest flavor of home') outshines flashy surface decoration.
